body_md:
\label{th:wsd}
Let $(\eta_j)$ be the WSD schedule with a cooldown length of $c$, and set
$\kappa_1 := 2-c-\gamma\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\big(1-\frac{2c}{3}\big)$ and
$\kappa_2 := c\big(1-\frac{\gamma\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)}{3}\big)$.
Under \cref{as:alphabeta} and \cref{as:eta}, as $T \to \infty$, we have
$B_T \sim \widetilde B_T$ and $V_T \sim \widetilde V_T$, where
\begin{align}
\widetilde B_T &:= \frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha}\,\Gamma(\omega) \,
  (\kappa_1 L\gamma T)^{-\omega},
  \label{eq:bias_equiv} \\
\widetilde V_T &:= \mathcal{W}_\gamma(\alpha,c)\,\sigma^2 (L\gamma)^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}\,
  T^{\frac{1}{\alpha}-1}
  \quad \text{if } 1<\alpha<2,
  \label{eq:var_equiv_small} \\
\widetilde V_T &:= \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{8}\,\zeta\big(\frac{\alpha}{2}\big)\,
  \sigma^2 (L\gamma/c)^{\frac12}\, T^{-\frac12}
  \quad \text{if } \alpha>2,
  \label{eq:var_equiv_large}
\end{align}
with \\
$\xi := 1/\alpha-1$, $\mathcal{I}_{\alpha,\gamma} := \int_0^1 x^{2\xi}(1-\gamma\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\,x/3)^{\xi-1}\,dx$
and $\mathcal{W}_\gamma(\alpha,c) := \frac{1}{2\alpha}\big[\frac{\Gamma(-\xi)}{2-\gamma\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)}(\kappa_2^{\xi}-\kappa_1^{\xi}) + \Gamma(1-\xi)\,\mathcal{I}_{\alpha,\gamma}\,c^{\xi}\big]$.

title: Lemma
body_md: Consider the function $f$ defined \cref{sec:setup}. Then $f$ is differentiable.

title: Proof
body_md:
Define the deterministic function $f_{u,v}$, for every $(u,v) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}$:
\[\begin{aligned}
    f_{u, v} \colon \mathbb{R}^d &\to \mathbb{R}, \\
    \theta &\mapsto \frac{1}{2}(u^\top \theta - v)^2.
\end{aligned}\]
Therefore $f(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[f_{x,y}(\theta)]$. To apply the dominated convergence theorem for differentiation, we verify the following conditions:

\begin{itemize}
    \item For all $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the expectation $\mathbb{E}[f_{x,y}(\theta)]$ is well-defined since $x$ and $y$ admit finite second-order moments.
    
    \item For all $(u,v) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}$, $f_{u, v}$ is continuously differentiable and its gradient is $\nabla f_{u,v}(\theta) = u(u^\top \theta-v)$.
    
    \item Let $R>0$. For all $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that $\|\theta\| \le R$, the gradient norm is bounded by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality:
    \[\|\nabla f_{x,y}(\theta)\| = \|x(x^\top \theta - y)\| \le \|x\|(\|x\| \|\theta\| + |y|) \le R\|x\|^2 + \|x\||y|.\]
    The random variable $R\|x\|^2 + \|x\||y|$ is integrable because $\mathbb{E}[\|x\|^2]$ is finite (since $H$ exists) and $\mathbb{E}[\|x\||y|]$ is finite (by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, as both $x$ and $y$ have finite second moments).
\end{itemize}

Thus, the local domination condition is met, which allows us to interchange the gradient and the expectation:
\[\nabla f(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[\nabla f_{x,y}(\theta)] = \mathbb{E}[x(x^\top \theta - y)].\]

Substituting $y = x^\top \theta_* + \varepsilon$, we get:
\[\nabla f(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[x(x^\top \theta - (x^\top \theta_* + \varepsilon))] = \mathbb{E}[x x^\top(\theta - \theta_*)] - \mathbb{E}[x\varepsilon].\]

body_md:
Let $M_t = Q^\top\mathbb{E}[(\theta_t-\theta_*)(\theta_t-\theta_*)^\top]Q$, and $m_t = \left(M_{i,i}\right)_{i\geq 1} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ the diagonal of $M_t$.
First, the risk can be written with $M_t$:
\begin{align*}
    \mathcal R_{t \mid T} &= \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[(\theta_t-\theta_*)^\top H(\theta_t-\theta_*)],
    \\&=
    \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Tr}\left( (\theta_t-\theta_*)(\theta_t-\theta_*)^\top H \right)],
    \\&=
    \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}(M_t\Lambda)
    = 
    \frac{1}{2}m_t ^\top \lambda.
\end{align*}

Thus $\mathcal R_{0 \mid T} = \frac{1}{2}\lambda^\top m_0$. By unwinding the recurrence for $m_t$ from \cref{lemma:recurrence}, we directly obtain:
    \[
    \mathcal R_{t \mid T} = \frac{1}{2}\lambda^\top \left( \prod_{k=0}^{t-1}[I - 2\gamma\eta_k\Lambda + \gamma^2\eta_k^2\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\Lambda]m_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\gamma^2\eta_k^2\sigma^2 \prod_{j=k+1}^{t-1}[I - 2\gamma\eta_j\Lambda + \gamma^2\eta_j^2\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\Lambda]\lambda  \right).
    \]

label: eq:Mt+1
title: Proof
body_md:
Without loss of generality, suppose $H$ is diagonal, i.e. $H=\Lambda$, and $\theta_* = 0$.
    Let us compute a recurrence relation with $M_t$.
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:Mt+1}
    \begin{aligned}
    M_{t+1} &= \mathbb{E}[((I-\gamma \eta_t x_t x_t^\top)\theta_t + \gamma \eta_t \varepsilon_t x_t)((I-\gamma \eta_t x_t x_t^\top)\theta_t + \gamma \eta_t \varepsilon_t x_t)^\top], \\
    &=  \mathbb{E}[(I-\gamma \eta_t x_t x_t^\top)\theta_t \theta_t^\top (I-\gamma \eta_t x_t x_t^\top)]+\gamma^2\eta_t^2\sigma^2 \Lambda,\\
    &=  \mathbb{E}[ (\theta_t-\gamma \eta_t x_t x_t^\top \theta_t)(\theta_t-\gamma \eta_t x_t x_t^\top \theta_t)^\top]  + \gamma^2\eta_t^2\sigma^2\Lambda, \qquad (\text{$\varepsilon_t$ and $x_t$ are independent and $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_t] =0$}),\\
    &= M_t - \gamma \eta_t \Lambda M_t - \gamma \eta_t M_t \Lambda + \gamma^2\eta_t^2  \mathbb{E}[x_t x_t^\top \theta_t \theta_t^\top x_t x_t^\top] + \gamma^2\eta_t^2\sigma^2\Lambda.
    \end{aligned}
    \end{equation}
    
    Moreover, the term $\mathbb{E}[x_t x_t^\top \theta_t \theta_t^\top x_t x_t^\top]$ can be computed using the distribution of $x_t$.
    \begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}[x_t x_t^\top \theta_t \theta_t^\top x_t x_t^\top| \theta_t] 
    &=
    \sum_{i\geq1} \frac{\lambda_i}{\mathrm{Tr} (\Lambda)} \times (\mathrm{Tr} (\Lambda))^2  e_i \underbrace{e_i^\top  \theta_t \theta_t^\top  e_i}_{=\theta_{t,i}^2} e_i^\top,
    \\&=
    \mathrm{Tr} (\Lambda)\sum_{i\geq1} \lambda_i \theta_{t,i}^2  e_i  e_i^\top
    =
    \mathrm{Tr} (\Lambda)
    \begin{pmatrix}
    \lambda_1 \theta_{t,1}^2 & 0                  & \cdots \\
    0                  & \lambda_2 \theta_{t,2}^2 & \cdots \\
    \vdots             & \vdots             & \ddots
    \end{pmatrix},
    \\&=
    \mathrm{Tr} (\Lambda) \Lambda \mathrm{Diag}(\theta_t)^2.
    \end{align*}
    
    Knowing that $\mathbb{E}[x_t x_t^\top \theta_t \theta_t^\top x_t x_t^\top] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[x_t x_t^\top \theta_t \theta_t^\top x_t x_t^\top | \theta_t]]$,
    \begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}[x_t x_t^\top \theta_t \theta_t^\top x_t x_t^\top] &= 
    \mathrm{Tr} (\Lambda) \Lambda \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Diag}(\theta_t)^2] ,
    \\&=
    \mathrm{Tr} (\Lambda) \Lambda \mathbb{E}\begin{pmatrix}
    \ \theta_{t,1}^2 & 0                  & \cdots \\
    0                  & \theta_{t,2}^2 & \cdots \\
    \vdots             & \vdots             & \ddots
    \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \mathrm{Tr} (\Lambda) \Lambda \begin{pmatrix}
    \ M_{t,11} & 0                  & \cdots \\
    0                  & M_{t,22} & \cdots \\
    \vdots             & \vdots             & \ddots
    \end{pmatrix},
    \\&= \mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\Lambda \mathrm{Diag}(m_t).
    \end{align*}
    Thus, substituting the result into \cref{eq:Mt+1},
    \begin{align*}
    M_{t+1} &=
    M_t - \gamma\eta_t \Lambda M_t - \gamma\eta_t M_t \Lambda + \gamma^2\eta_t^2 \mathrm{Tr} (\Lambda) \Lambda \mathrm{Diag}(m_t) + \gamma^2\eta_t^2\sigma^2\Lambda.
    \end{align*}

    Hence,
    $\begin{aligned}[t]
    m_{t+1} &= m_t - 2 \gamma \eta_t \Lambda m_t +  \gamma^2\eta_t^2  \mathrm{Tr} (\Lambda) \Lambda m_t + \gamma^2\eta_t^2\sigma^2\lambda,
    \\&=
    \left[I + (-2\gamma \eta_t   + \gamma^2\eta_t^2 \mathrm{Tr} (\Lambda)) \Lambda  \right]m_t + \gamma^2\eta_t^2\sigma^2\lambda.
    \end{aligned}$

name: \textcite{korevaar2004tauberian}, Theorem 7.4, Part I. See also \textcite{bach2025ztransform

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\bar \gamma  = \gamma  - \frac{\gamma ^2 \mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)}{2}$. By \cref{as:eta}, $0<\bar\gamma  < \frac{1}{2L}$.

        \paragraph{Bias.}
        The exact bias for a horizon $T$ is:
        \[
        B_T = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i^{\infty} \frac{L\Delta}{i^{\alpha+\beta}} [1 - 2\bar\gamma \frac{L}{i^{\alpha}}]^T.
        \]
        
        The $z$-transform is
        \[
        \mathcal B(z) = \sum_{T=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2}\sum_i^{\infty} \frac{L\Delta}{i^{\alpha+\beta}} [1 - 2\bar\gamma \frac{L}{i^{\alpha}}]^T z^T
        =
        \frac{L\Delta}{2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty  \frac{1}{i^{\alpha+\beta}} \frac{1}{1-z[1 - 2\bar\gamma \frac{L}{i^{\alpha}}]}.
       \]
        
        As $z \to 1$, $\frac{1}{i^{\alpha+\beta}} \frac{1}{1-z[1 - 2\bar\gamma \frac{L}{i^{\alpha}}]} \sim \frac{1}{i^{\alpha+\beta}} \frac{1}{ 2\bar\gamma \frac{L}{i^{\alpha}}} \sim \frac{1}{2L\bar\gamma  i^\beta}$. If $\beta >1, \sum_i \frac{1}{2L\bar\gamma  i^\beta}$ converges. We force the $z$-transform to diverge in differentiating $\mathcal B$.
        \begin{align*}
        \mathcal B^{(\mu)}(z) &=
        \frac{L\Delta}{2} \sum_{i=1}^\infty i^{-(\alpha+\beta)} \frac{\mu! (1 - 2\bar{\gamma } L i^{-\alpha})^\mu}{\left[ 1 - z(1 - 2\bar{\gamma } L i^{-\alpha}) \right]^{\mu+1}}.
        \end{align*}
        
        So with the right $\mu \in \mathbb N_{\geq0}$, we can have $\mu\alpha - \beta >-1$ (e.g. $\mu =\lfloor \frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}\rfloor+1$) so that $\mathcal B^{(\mu)}(z)$ diverges when $z\to 1$, to be able to apply Tauberian theorems. With $s = 1-z >0$,
        \begin{align*}
        i^{-(\alpha+\beta)} \frac{\mu! (1 - 2\bar{\gamma } L i^{-\alpha})^\mu}{\left[ 1 - z(1 - 2\bar{\gamma } L i^{-\alpha}) \right]^{\mu+1}} &\sim 
        \frac{\mu!}{[i^{\alpha}s + (1-s)2\bar \gamma  L]^{\mu+1}} i^{\mu\alpha-\beta}.
        \end{align*}
        
        By substituting $i = x_i s^{-1/\alpha}$ and forcing the appearance of the step size $\Delta x = s^{1/\alpha}$, we can reformulate the sum to reveal a Riemann sum structure:
        \begin{align*} 
        \mathcal B^{(\mu)}(1-s) &\sim
        \frac{L\Delta}{2} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{\mu!}{[ (x_i s^{-1/\alpha})^\alpha s + (1-s)2\bar \gamma  L]^{\mu+1}} (x_i s^{-1/\alpha})^{\mu\alpha-\beta},
        \\&=
        \frac{L\Delta}{2} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{\mu!}{[x_i^\alpha + (1-s)2\bar \gamma  L]^{\mu+1}} x_i^{\mu\alpha-\beta} s^{-\mu + \frac{\beta}{\alpha}},
        \\&=
        \frac{L\Delta}{2} s^{\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha} - \mu} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{\mu!}{[x_i^\alpha + (1-s)2\bar \gamma  L]^{\mu+1}} x_i^{\mu\alpha-\beta} \underbrace{s^{1/\alpha}}_{=\Delta x}.
        \end{align*}
        
        As $s \to 0$, we have $(1-s)2\bar\gamma  L \to 2\bar\gamma  L$. The discrete sum is exactly a Riemann sum with a vanishing step size $\Delta x \to 0$. It converges to the continuous integral over $[0, \infty)$:
        \begin{align*}
        \mathcal B^{(\mu)}(1-s) &\sim
        \frac{L\Delta}{2} s^{\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha} - \mu} \int_0^\infty \frac{\mu!}{[x^\alpha + 2\bar \gamma  L]^{\mu+1}} x^{\mu\alpha-\beta} dx.
        \end{align*}
        
        We directly apply the substitution $v = \frac{x^\alpha}{2\bar\gamma  L}$, which gives $dx = \frac{1}{\alpha} (2\bar\gamma  L)^{1/\alpha} v^{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}} dv$:
        \begin{align*}
        \mathcal B^{(\mu)}(1-s) &\sim
        \frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha} \mu! \, s^{\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}-\mu} \int_0^\infty \frac{(2\bar\gamma  L v)^{\mu - \frac{\beta}{\alpha}}}{[2\bar\gamma  L(v + 1)]^{\mu+1}} (2\bar\gamma  L)^{1/\alpha} v^{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}} dv,
        \\&=
        \frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha} \mu! \, s^{\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}-\mu} (2\bar\gamma  L)^{\mu - \frac{\beta}{\alpha} - \mu - 1 + \frac{1}{\alpha}} \int_0^\infty \frac{v^{-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}-1+\mu}}{[v + 1]^{\mu+1}} dv,
        \\&=
        \frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha} \mu! \, s^{\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}-\mu} (2\bar{\gamma }L)^{-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}-1} \frac{\Gamma(\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}+1)\Gamma(\mu-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha})}{\Gamma(\mu+1)},
        \\\mathcal B^{(\mu)}(z)&\sim
        \frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha} (2\bar{\gamma }L)^{-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}-1} \Gamma\left(\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}+1\right)\Gamma\left(\mu-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}\right) (1-z)^{-\left(\mu-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}\right)}.
        \end{align*}
        

        We have shown that 
        $\lim_{z \to 1^-} (1-z)^{\mu-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}} \mathcal B^{(\mu)}(z) = \frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha} (2\bar{\gamma }L)^{-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}-1} \Gamma\left(\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}+1\right)\Gamma\left(\mu-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}\right)$. 
        Moreover, $T^{2+\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}} (B_T - B_{T-1} ) \leq 0$ since $(B_T)$ is decreasing. Indeed, each term $[1-2\bar\gamma\frac{L}{i^\alpha}]^T$ is decreasing in $T$ since $\forall i\geq 1, [1-2\bar\gamma\frac{L}{i^\alpha}] \in (0,1)$ from \cref{as:eta}. Applying \cref{th:tauberian},   
        \[ 
        \lim_{z \to 1^-} (1-z)^{\mu-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}} \mathcal B^{(\mu)}(z) = \Gamma({\mu-\tfrac{\beta-1}{\alpha}} ) \cdot \lim_{T \to +\infty} T^{1+\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}} B_T.
        \]
        As $T\to\infty$, this is equivalent to:
        \begin{align*}
        B_T &\sim \frac{1}{\Gamma\left(\mu-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}\right)} \left[ \frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha} (2\bar{\gamma }L)^{-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}-1} \Gamma\left(\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}+1\right)\Gamma\left(\mu-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}\right) \right] T^{-\left(\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}+1\right)},
        \\
         &\sim \frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha} (2\bar{\gamma }L)^{-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}-1} \Gamma\left(\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}+1\right) T^{-\left(\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}+1\right)},
        \\
         &\sim \frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha} \frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}+1\right)}{(2\bar{\gamma }L T)^{\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}+1}}.
        \end{align*}



    \paragraph{Variance.}
    \[
        V_T = \frac{\gamma ^2 \sigma^2}{4\bar\gamma } \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} L i^{-\alpha} \left[ 1 - (1 - 2\bar\gamma  L i^{-\alpha})^T \right].
    \]
    Therefore, since $|1-2\bar\gamma  Li^{-\alpha}|<1$ and $\left[ 1 - (1 - 2\bar\gamma  L i^{-\alpha})^T \right]$ is dominated,
    \[
        \lim_{T \to \infty} V_T = \frac{\gamma ^2 \sigma^2 L}{4\bar\gamma } \zeta(\alpha) \qquad \text{with }\bar\gamma  = \gamma  -\frac{ \gamma ^2\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)}{2}.
    \]

title: Proof
body_md:
We have:
\[\left\{\begin{aligned}
\eta_k &=  1 - \frac{k}{T}, \\
\bar\nu_k &= \frac{2\gamma\eta_k - \gamma^2\eta_k^2\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)}{2} = \gamma\eta_k - \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\gamma^2\eta_k^2, \\
\Pi_{T,i} &= \prod_{k=0}^{T-1} \left[ 1 - 2\bar\nu_k \frac{L}{i^\alpha} \right].
\end{aligned}\right.\]




By \cref{as:eta}, $\bar\gamma = \frac{2\gamma - \gamma^2\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)}{2} <\frac{1}{2L}$. Then $\forall i\geq1, \forall  k\in\{1,...,T\}, 1 - 2\bar\nu_k \frac{L}{i^\alpha}  \geq0$.


\paragraph{Tauberian condition.} Let $p_0 := 1 - 1/\zeta(\alpha) > 0$ and $\delta := 2 - \gamma\,\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda) > 0$. For $\eta \in [0,1]$, the factor $P_i(\eta) := 1 - 2\gamma\eta\lambda_i + \gamma^2\eta^2\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\lambda_i$ satisfies $P_i(\eta) \geq p_0$, $|P_i'(\eta)| \leq 2\gamma\lambda_i$ and $1 - P_i(\eta) \geq \delta\gamma\lambda_i\eta$. Since $|\eta^{(T)}_k - \eta^{(T-1)}_k| \leq \frac{k}{cT(T-1)}$ for $k \leq T-2$ (also for WSD, with $\eta^{(T)}_k = \min(1, \frac{T-k}{cT})$), we get
\[
  \big|\log (\Pi_{T,i}) - \log (\Pi_{T-1,i})\big| \leq \frac{2\gamma\lambda_i}{p_0}\Big(\frac{1}{2c} + 1\Big) =: C_1\gamma\lambda_i ,
\]
which is bounded, hence $|\Pi_{T,i} - \Pi_{T-1,i}| \leq C_2\,\gamma\lambda_i\,\Pi_{T-1,i}$. Moreover, $\sum_{k} \eta^{(T-1)}_k \geq (T-1)/2$ gives $\Pi_{T-1,i} \leq e^{-\delta\gamma\lambda_i (T-1)/2}$. Therefore
\[
  |B_T - B_{T-1}| \leq C_3 \sum_{i \geq 1} i^{-2\alpha-\beta}\, e^{-\delta\gamma L T i^{-\alpha}/2} = O\big(T^{-1-\omega}\big),
\]
   by comparison with $\int_0^\infty x^{-2\alpha-\beta} e^{-aTx^{-\alpha}}\,dx = \frac{\Gamma(\omega+1)}{\alpha}(aT)^{-1-\omega}$, where $a := \delta\gamma L/2$. Hence the condition of \cref{th:tauberian} for the bias, $T^{1+\omega}(B_T - B_{T-1}) \leq K$, holds for all $\gamma < 2/\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)$. 
For the variance, write $V_T = \frac12\sum_i w_i \sum_{\ell=1}^{T} \eta_T(\ell)^2\, \Pi_T(\ell)$, where $w_i := L^2\gamma^2\sigma^2 i^{-2\alpha}$, $\eta_T(\ell) := \min(1, \frac{\ell}{cT})$ is the step size $\ell$ steps before the end, and $\Pi_T(\ell) := \prod_{\ell' < \ell} P_i(\eta_T(\ell'))$. Aligning the two horizons from the end, $0 \leq \eta_{T-1}(\ell) - \eta_T(\ell) \leq \eta_{T-1}(\ell)/T$, so that, with $E(\ell) := \sum_{\ell' < \ell} \eta_{T-1}(\ell')$, we have $|\log (\Pi_T(\ell)) - \log (\Pi_{T-1}(\ell))| \leq \frac{2\gamma\lambda_i}{p_0 T} E(\ell)$ and $\Pi_{T-1}(\ell) \leq e^{-\delta\gamma\lambda_i E(\ell)}$. Hence, for $T$ large enough,
\[
  |V_T - V_{T-1}| \leq \frac{C}{T} \sum_{i} w_i \sum_{\ell < T} \eta_{T-1}(\ell)^2\, e^{-\delta\gamma\lambda_i E(\ell)/2} + \frac12 \sum_i w_i\, e^{-\delta\gamma\lambda_i (T-1)/2},
\]
the last term coming from the additional step. Since $E(\ell) \geq \frac{\ell(\ell-1)}{2cT}$ for $\ell \leq cT$ and $E(\ell) \geq \ell - \frac{cT}{2} - 2$ otherwise, the first double sum is $O(T^{p-1})$, as for $\widetilde V_T$: modes $i \gtrsim T^{1/\alpha}$ contribute $O(T^{1/\alpha - 1})$, and modes $i \lesssim T^{1/\alpha}$ contribute $O\big(T^{-1/2}\sum_{i \lesssim T^{1/\alpha}} i^{-\alpha/2}\big)$. The second sum is $O(T^{1/\alpha - 2})$. Therefore $T^{2-p}|V_T - V_{T-1}| \leq K$, with $p = 1/\alpha$ if $\alpha < 2$ and $p = 1/2$ if $\alpha > 2$.

\paragraph{Bias.}



Let $j = T - k$. As $k$ goes from $0$ to $T-1$, $j$ goes from $T$ down to $1$, and $1 - \frac{k}{T} = \frac{j}{T}$.


\begin{align*}
1 - 2\bar\nu_k \frac{L}{i^\alpha} &= 1 - \frac{2L}{i^\alpha} \left[ \gamma   \left(\frac{j}{T}\right) - \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\gamma  ^2 \left(\frac{j}{T}\right)^2 \right] = 1 - \underbrace{\frac{2\gamma   L}{i^\alpha}}_{A^{(1)}_i=i^{-\alpha}A^{(1)}} \left(\frac{j}{T}\right) + \underbrace{\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\gamma  ^2 L}{i^\alpha}}_{A^{(2)}_i = i^{-\alpha}A^{(2)}} \left(\frac{j}{T}\right)^2.
\end{align*}
Therefore,
\begin{align*}
\Pi_{T,i} &= \prod_{j=1}^{T} \left[ \frac{A^{(2)}_i}{T^2} j^2 - \frac{A^{(1)}_i}{T} j + 1 \right] = \left( \frac{A^{(2)}_i}{T^2} \right)^T \prod_{j=1}^{T} \left( j^2 - \frac{A^{(1)}_i T}{A^{(2)}_i} j + \frac{T^2}{A^{(2)}_i} \right),
\\&=
({A^{(2)}_i})^T \prod_{j=1}^{T} \left( \left(\frac{j}{T}\right)^2 - \frac{A^{(1)}_i }{A^{(2)}_i} \left(\frac{j}{T}\right) + \frac{1}{A^{(2)}_i} \right)=
 \exp\left[\sum_{j=1}^{T} \log\left( A^{(2)}_i\left(\frac{j}{T}\right)^2 - A^{(1)}_i \left(\frac{j}{T}\right) + 1\right)\right],
\\&\sim \sqrt{A^{(2)}_i-A^{(1)}_i+1}\exp\left[T\int_{0}^{1} \log\left( A^{(2)}_iu^2 - A^{(1)}_iu + 1\right)du\right].
\end{align*}

By Euler-Maclaurin, $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^{T} f\left(\frac{j}{T}\right) = T\int_{0}^{1} f(u)du + \frac{f(1)-f(0)}{2} + r_{i,T}$ 
and $r_{i,T} = O(\frac{i^{-\alpha}}{T}).$


Let $S_{i,T} = \Pi_{T,i}\exp\left[-T\int_{0}^{1} \log\left( A^{(2)}_iu^2 - A^{(1)}_iu + 1\right)du\right] = e^{r_{i,T}}\sqrt{A^{(2)}_i-A^{(1)}_i+1} \to 1$ as $i\to \infty$.

$S_i := \lim_{T\to \infty} S_{i,T} = \sqrt{A^{(2)}_i-A^{(1)}_i+1}$. The convergence is uniform with respect to $i$.
As $z\to 1$,
\begin{align*}
\mathcal B(z) &= \frac{L\Delta}{2}\sum_{T=0}^\infty \sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{S_{i,T}}{i^{\alpha+\beta}}e^{T\int_0^1\log(\frac{A^{(2)}}{i^\alpha}u^2 - \frac{A^{(1)}}{i^\alpha}u+1)du}z^T,
\\&
\sim \frac{L\Delta}{2} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{S_i}{i^{\alpha+\beta}} \frac{1}{1-ze^{\int_0^1\log(\frac{A^{(2)}}{i^\alpha}u^2 - \frac{A^{(1)}}{i^\alpha}u+1)du}},
\end{align*}
the inversion being possible by Fubini's theorem (all terms are positive).


Let us take the $\mu$-th derivative of $\mathcal B$  so that $\mathcal B^{(\mu)}(z)$ diverges as $z \to 1$.

$\displaystyle \mathcal B(z) = \frac{L\Delta}{2} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \sum_{T=0}^\infty \frac{S_{i,T}}{i^{\alpha+\beta}} e^{TI_i}z^T$ so $\displaystyle\mathcal B'(z) =  \frac{L\Delta}{2} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \sum_{T=1}^\infty \frac{TS_{i,T}}{i^{\alpha+\beta}} e^{TI_i}z^{T-1}$. 

We can iterate this $\mu$ times and we get $(z \to 1)$:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal B^{(\mu)}(z) \sim \frac{L\Delta}{2} \mu! \sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{S_i}{i^{\alpha+\beta}} \frac{\left(e^{I_i}\right)^\mu}{\left(1 - z e^{I_i}\right)^{\mu+1}}.
\end{align*}

First, $S_i = 1+ O(i^{-\alpha})$. Second, we know that $\int_0^1\ln(\frac{A^{(2)}}{i^\alpha}u^2 - \frac{A^{(1)}}{i^\alpha}u+1)du = \frac{A^{(2)}}{3i^\alpha} - \frac{A^{(1)}}{2i^\alpha} + O(i^{-2\alpha})$ so $e^{I_i} = 1 - Ci^{-\alpha}+O(i^{-2\alpha})$ with $C=\frac{A^{(1)}}{2}-\frac{A^{(2)}}{3}$.



By defining $x_i = i s^{1/\alpha}$ and forcing the step size $\Delta x = s^{1/\alpha}$, we can reformulate the sum for large $i$ (where $S_i \to 1$):
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{B}^{(\mu)}(1-s) &\sim 
\frac{L\Delta}{2} \mu! \sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{ (1+O((x_is^{-1/\alpha})^{-\alpha}))(x_i s^{-1/\alpha})^{-(\alpha+\beta)} }{ [s + (1-s)( C (x_i s^{-1/\alpha})^{-\alpha}+O((x_is^{-1/\alpha})^{-2\alpha}))]^{\mu+1} },
\\&=
\frac{L\Delta}{2} \mu! \sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{(1+O(x_i^{-\alpha}s)) x_i^{-(\alpha+\beta)} s^{1 + \frac{\beta}{\alpha}} }{ [s + (1-s) C x_i^{-\alpha} s +O(x_i^{-2\alpha}s^2)]^{\mu+1} },
\\&=
\frac{L\Delta}{2} \mu! \sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{(1+O(x_i^{-\alpha}s))  x_i^{-(\alpha+\beta)} s^{1 + \frac{\beta}{\alpha}} }{ s^{\mu+1} [1 + (1-s) C x_i^{-\alpha}+ O(x_i^{-2\alpha}s) ]^{\mu+1} }.
\end{align*}

To recognize the standard Riemann form, we multiply the numerator and denominator by $x_i^{\alpha(\mu+1)}$:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{B}^{(\mu)}(1-s) &\sim
\frac{L\Delta}{2} \mu! \, s^{\frac{\beta}{\alpha} - \mu} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{(1+O(x_i^{-\alpha}s))  x_i^{\alpha\mu - \beta} }{ [x_i^\alpha + (1-s) C + O(x_i^{-\alpha}s) ]^{\mu+1} },
\\&=
\frac{L\Delta}{2} \mu! \, s^{\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha} - \mu} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \underbrace{ \frac{ (1+O(x_i^{-\alpha}s)) x_i^{\alpha\mu - \beta} }{ [x_i^\alpha + (1-s) C + O(x_i^{-\alpha}s)]^{\mu+1} }  }_{=:U_i}\underbrace{s^{1/\alpha}}_{= \Delta x}.
\end{align*}

Set $
\begin{aligned}[t] g_s : 
[0,\infty) &\to \mathbb{R},\\ x &\mapsto U_i 
\end{aligned}$ with $i = \lceil x s^{-1/\alpha}\rceil $. 
Then $g_s(x_i) = U_i$, and since $s^{1/\alpha} = \Delta x$,
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^\infty  \frac{ x_i^{\alpha\mu - \beta} }{ [x_i^\alpha + (1-s) C + O(x_i^{-\alpha}s)]^{\mu+1} } s^{1/\alpha} =  \int_{0}^\infty  g_s(u) du.
\]

For every $x \in [0,\infty)$, $g_s(x) \xrightarrow{s\to0} \frac{x^{\alpha\mu-\beta}}{(x^\alpha +C)^{\mu+1}}$. By the dominated convergence theorem,
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{B}^{(\mu)}(1-s) &\sim
\frac{L\Delta}{2} \mu! \, s^{\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha} - \mu} \int_0^\infty \frac{x^{\alpha\mu - \beta}}{[x^\alpha + C]^{\mu+1}} dx.
\end{align*}



Therefore as $s \to 0$,
\begin{align*}
\mathcal B^{(\mu)} \sim \frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha} C^{-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}-1} \Gamma\left(\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}+1\right)\Gamma\left(\mu - \frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}\right) s^{\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha} - \mu}.
\end{align*}

Moreover, the Tauberian condition established above gives $T^{1+\omega}(B_T-B_{T-1}) \le K$, so \cref{th:tauberian} applies with $p = \mu - \frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}$ (so that $2+\mu-p = 1+\omega$ and $1+\mu-p = \omega$):
\[
\lim_{z\to 1^-} (1-z)^{\mu-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}}\,\mathcal B^{(\mu)}(z)
= \Gamma\Big(\mu-\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}\Big)\lim_{T\to\infty} T^{\omega} B_T ,
\]
hence
\[
B_T \sim \frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha} \frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha} + 1\right)}{\left[ \gamma  L T \left( 1 - \frac{\gamma  Tr(\Lambda)}{3} \right) \right]^{\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha} + 1}}.
\]


\paragraph{Variance.}


The variance is defined as 
\[
V_T = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^{T-1}  \frac{L^2}{i^{2\alpha}}\gamma^2\eta_k^2 \sigma^2 \prod_{m=k+1}^{T-1} \left[ 1 - 2\bar{\nu}_m \frac{L}{i^\alpha} \right].
\]

The same method can be used for the product.
Let $j = T-m$.
\[
\prod_{m=k+1}^{T-1} \left[ 1 - 2\bar{\nu}_m \frac{L}{i^\alpha} \right] 
=
\prod_{j=1}^{T-k-1} \left[ 1 - 2\bar{\nu}_{T-j} \frac{L}{i^\alpha} \right] =
\exp\left[\sum_{j=1}^{T-k-1} \log\left( A^{(2)}_i\left(\frac{j}{T}\right)^2 - A^{(1)}_i \left(\frac{j}{T}\right) + 1\right)\right].
\]


By Euler-MacLaurin, 
\begin{multline*}\sum_{j=1}^{T-k-1} \log\left( A^{(2)}_i\left(\frac{j}{T}\right)^2 - A^{(1)}_i \left(\frac{j}{T}\right) + 1\right) = T \int_0^{1-\frac{k+1}{T}} \log\left( A^{(2)}_i u^2 - A^{(1)}_i u + 1 \right) du  \\+ \frac{\log(A^{(2)}_i v_k^2 - A^{(1)}_i v_k + 1)}{2} +o(1).\end{multline*}

Hence,
\[
\prod_{m=k+1}^{T-1} \left[ 1 - 2\bar{\nu}_m \frac{L}{i^\alpha} \right]= \underbrace{(1+o(1))\sqrt{A^{(2)}_i v_k^2 - A^{(1)}_i v_k + 1}}_{S_{i,k} \xrightarrow{i} 1}  \exp\left[ T \int_0^{1-\frac{k+1}{T}} \log\left( A^{(2)}_i u^2 - A^{(1)}_i u + 1 \right) du \right],
\]
with $v_k = 1 - \frac{k+1}{T}$.
Let $\ell = T - k$ and $x = \frac{\ell-1}{T}$. The sum over $\ell$ is a Riemann's sum, so
\begin{align*}
V_T &= \sum_{i=1}^\infty \sum_{\ell=1}^{T} \frac{L^2}{i^{2\alpha}}\gamma ^2 \sigma^2 \left(\frac{\ell}{T}\right)^2 S_{i,T-\ell} \exp\left[ T \int_0^{\frac{\ell-1}{T}} \log\left( A^{(2)}_i u^2 - A^{(1)}_i u + 1 \right) du \right], \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^\infty T \int_0^1 \frac{L^2}{i^{2\alpha}}\gamma ^2 \sigma^2 x^2 S_{i,T(1-x)}\exp\left[ T \int_0^{x} \log\left( A^{(2)}_i u^2 - A^{(1)}_i u + 1 \right) du \right] dx +O(1/T).
\end{align*}


\paragraph{Case $1 < \alpha < 2$:}


Knowing that $S_{i,k} = 1+O(i^{-\alpha})$ uniformly, the $z$-transform is:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal V(z) &=  \frac{1}{2} \sum_{T=0}^\infty \left( \sum_{i=1}^\infty \int_0^1 \frac{L^2}{i^{2\alpha}}\gamma ^2 \sigma^2 x^2  (1+O(
i^{-\alpha}))\exp\left[ T \int_0^{x-\frac{1}{T}} \log\left( A^{(2)}_i u^2 - A^{(1)}_i u + 1 \right) du \right] dx + O(1/T) \right)z^T, 
\\&=
\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=0}^\infty \int_0^1 \frac{L^2}{i^{2\alpha}}\gamma ^2 \sigma^2 x^2 (1+O(
i^{-\alpha}))  \frac{ze^{I_i(x)}}{(1-ze^{I_i(x)})^2} dx + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{T=0}^\infty O(1/T)z^T}_{=:R(z)}.
\end{align*}

Indeed, $\sum_{T=0}^\infty T y^T = \sum_{T=0}^\infty y\frac{d}{dy}y^{T} = y\frac{d}{dy} \frac{1}{1-y} = \frac{y}{(1-y)^2} $. For $i \to \infty$,
\begin{align*}
I_i(x) &= \int_0^{x}\log\left( A^{(2)}_i u^2 - A^{(1)}_i u + 1 \right) du 
= \int_0^{x} A^{(2)}_i u^2 - A^{(1)}_i u + O(i^{-2\alpha})du ,
\\&= i^{-\alpha}\left(\frac{A^{(2)}}{3}x^3 - \frac{A^{(1)}}{2}x^2\right) + O(i^{-2\alpha})
=
-i^{-\alpha}C(x) +O(i^{-2\alpha}),
\end{align*}
Where $C(x) = -\frac{A^{(2)}}{3}x^3 + \frac{A^{(1)}}{2}x^2$.


\begin{align*}
\mathcal V(z)-R(z) &=\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \int_0^1 \frac{L^2}{i^{2\alpha}}\gamma ^2 \sigma^2 x^2 (1+O(
i^{-\alpha}))\frac{ze^{I_i(x)}}{(1-ze^{I_i(x)})^2} dx ,
\\&=
\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty \int_0^1 \frac{L^2}{i^{2\alpha}}\gamma ^2 \sigma^2 x^2  (1+O(
i^{-\alpha}))\frac{(1-s)e^{I_i(x)}}{(1-(1-s)(1-i^{-\alpha}C(x) +O(i^{-2\alpha})))^2} dx,
\\&=
\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty \int_0^1 \frac{L^2}{i^{2\alpha}}\gamma ^2 \sigma^2 x^2 \frac{1+O(i^{-\alpha})}{(s + (1-s)i^{-\alpha}C(x)+O(i^{-2\alpha}))^2} dx,
\\&=
\frac{1}{2}\int_0^1 L^2 \gamma ^2 \sigma^2   \sum_{i=1}^\infty  \frac{x^2}{i^{2\alpha}} \frac{1+O(i^{-\alpha})}{(s + (1-s)i^{-\alpha}C(x)+O(i^{-2\alpha}))^2} dx.
\end{align*}

Here the sum diverges when $z \to 1$, so there is no need to differentiate $\mathcal V-R$. We then have to turn the sum into an integral.
Set $x_i = is^{1/\alpha}$. Therefore $\Delta x_i = s^{1/\alpha}$.



\begin{align*}
\mathcal V(z) -R(z)& =
\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty \int_0^1 L^2 \gamma ^2 \sigma^2    \frac{u^2}{(x_is^{-1/\alpha})^{2\alpha}} \frac{1+O((x_is^{-1/\alpha})^{-\alpha})}{(s + (1-s) (x_is^{-1/\alpha})^{-\alpha}C(u)+O((x_is^{-1/\alpha})^{-2\alpha}))^2} du,
\\&=
\frac{L^2 \gamma ^2 \sigma^2}{2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty \int_0^1     \frac{u^2}{x_i^{2\alpha}s^{-2}} \frac{1+O(x_i^{-\alpha}s)}{(s + (1-s) x_i^{-\alpha}sC(u)+O(x_i^{-2\alpha}s^{2}))^2} du,
\\&=
\frac{L^2 \gamma ^2 \sigma^2}{2}s^{-1/\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^\infty \underbrace{\int_0^1     \frac{u^2}{x_i^{2\alpha}} \frac{1+O(x_i^{-\alpha}s)}{(1 + (1-s) x_i^{-\alpha}C(u)+O(x_i^{-2\alpha}s))^2} s^{1/\alpha}du}_{=:U_i(s)}.
\end{align*}


Set $g_s : 
\begin{aligned}[t]
[0,\infty) &\to \mathbb{R},\\ x &\mapsto U_i(s)
\end{aligned}$ with $i = \lceil x s^{-1/\alpha}\rceil $. Then $\int_0^\infty g_s(x)dx = \sum_{i=1}^\infty U_i(s)$.

Moreover, $\displaystyle \forall i\geq1, g_s(x) \xrightarrow{s\to0}\int_0^1 \frac{u^2}{x^{2\alpha}}\frac{1}{(1+x^{-\alpha}C(u))^2}du.$


By the Dominated convergence theorem,
\[\sum_{i=1}U_i(s) \xrightarrow{s\to 0} \int_0^\infty\int_0^1 \frac{u^2}{x^{2\alpha}}\frac{1}{(1+x^{-\alpha}C(u))^2}dudx.
\]

\bigskip

Let $w = C(u)x^{-\alpha}$, then $dx = -\frac{1}{\alpha} C(u)^{1/\alpha} w^{-1/\alpha - 1} dw$.
\begin{align*}
\int_{0}^\infty \frac{x^{-2\alpha}}{(1 + C(u)x^{-\alpha})^2} dx
&= \int_{0}^\infty \frac{C(u)^{-2} w^2}{(1+w)^2} \left( \frac{1}{\alpha} C(u)^{1/\alpha} w^{-1/\alpha - 1} \right) dw,
\\&= \frac{1}{\alpha} C(u)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} \int_0^\infty \frac{w^{1-1/\alpha}}{(1+w)^2} dw,
\\&= \frac{1}{\alpha} C(u)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} \Gamma\left(2 - \frac{1}{\alpha}\right) \Gamma\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\right).
\end{align*}

Therefore, the behavior of the z-transform is:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal V(1-s) - R(1-s) &\sim \frac{L^2 \gamma ^2 \sigma^2 }{2\alpha}s^{-1/\alpha}   \Gamma\left(2 - \frac{1}{\alpha}\right) \Gamma\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\right) \int_0^1 u^2 C(u)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} du .
\end{align*}

By the Tauberian theorem, if $\mathcal V(1-s)-R(1-s) \sim K s^{-\omega}$ with $\omega = \frac{1}{\alpha} > 0$, then the $T$-th coefficient behaves as $V_T-O(1/T) \sim \frac{K}{\Gamma(\omega)} T^{\omega - 1}$.
\begin{align*}
V_T -O(1/T)&\sim \frac{1}{\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)} \left[ \frac{L^2 \gamma ^2 \sigma^2 }{2\alpha} \Gamma\left(2 - \frac{1}{\alpha}\right) \Gamma\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\right) \int_0^1 u^2 C(u)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} du \right] T^{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}} ,
\\
V_T&\sim \frac{L^2 \gamma ^2 \sigma^2}{2\alpha} \Gamma\left(2 - \frac{1}{\alpha}\right) \left( \int_0^1 u^2 C(u)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} du \right) T^{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}}.
\end{align*}
Because $O(1/T)$ is negligible before $T^{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}}$.

We can now substitute $C(u)$ into the temporal integral and factor out the leading terms:
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1 u^2 C(u)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} du &= \int_0^1 u^2 \left( \frac{A^{(1)}}{2}u^2 - \frac{A^{(2)}}{3}u^3 \right)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} du ,
\\&= \left(\frac{A^{(1)}}{2}\right)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} \int_0^1 u^2 \cdot u^{2\left(\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}\right)} \left( 1 - \frac{2A^{(2)}}{3A^{(1)}}u \right)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} du ,
\\&= \left(\frac{A^{(1)}}{2}\right)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} \int_0^1 u^{\frac{2-2\alpha}{\alpha}} \left( 1 - \frac{2A^{(2)}}{3A^{(1)}}u \right)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} du.
\end{align*}

Let $\mathcal{I}_{\alpha, \gamma } = \int_0^1 u^{\frac{2-2\alpha}{\alpha}} \left( 1 - \frac{\gamma  \mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)}{3} u \right)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} du$ .

The final asymptotic equivalent for the variance under a linear schedule is therefore :
\begin{align*}V_T &\sim  \frac{L^2 \gamma ^2 \sigma^2}{2\alpha} \Gamma\left(2 - \frac{1}{\alpha}\right) \left(\gamma  L\right)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} \mathcal{I}_{\alpha, \gamma } T^{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}}, \qquad \text{if }1<\alpha<2.
\end{align*}



\paragraph{Case $\alpha > 2$.}
The spectral tail decays too rapidly; the integral $\mathcal{I}_{\alpha, \gamma }$ diverges.

This time, we cannot concentrate on large $i$. However, with a fixed $i$, knowing $C(u) =\gamma  L u^2 +O(u^3)$ as $u \to 0$, we can cut the integral along $u$.
\begin{align*}
\mathcal V(z)-R(z) &= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \int_0^1 \frac{L^2}{i^{2\alpha}}\gamma ^2 \sigma^2 u^2   S_{i,T(1-u)}\frac{ze^{I_i(u)}}{(1-ze^{I_i(u)})^2} du,
\\
&=
\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \int_0^1 \frac{L^2}{i^{2\alpha}}\gamma ^2 \sigma^2 u^2 (1+O(i^{-\alpha}u))\frac{ze^{I_i(u)}}{(1-ze^{I_i(u)})^2} du,
\\&=
\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \int_0^1 \frac{L^2}{i^{2\alpha}}\gamma ^2 \sigma^2 u^2 (1+O(i^{-\alpha}u))\frac{z(1-C(u)i^{-\alpha}+O(i^{-\alpha}u^2))}{(1-z(1-C(u)i^{-\alpha}+O(i^{-\alpha}u^2)))^2} du,
\\
\mathcal V(1-s) - R(1-s)&=
\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \int_0^1 \frac{L^2}{i^{2\alpha}}\gamma ^2 \sigma^2 u^2 (1+O(i^{-\alpha}u))\frac{(1-s)(1-C(u)i^{-\alpha}+O(i^{-\alpha}u^2))}{(1-(1-s)(1-C(u)i^{-\alpha}+O(i^{-\alpha}u^2)))^2} du.
\end{align*}

Let $u = s^{1/2} w$. $du=s^{1/2}dw$,
\begin{align*}
\mathcal V(1-s) - R(1-s) 
&= \frac{L^2 \gamma ^2 \sigma^2}{2} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{1}{i^{2\alpha}} \int_0^{s^{-1/2}} \frac{sw^2 \left(1 + {O}(s + i^{-\alpha}s^{1/2}w)\right)}{\left(s + (1-s)i^{-\alpha}C(s^{1/2}w) + {O}(i^{-\alpha}sw^2)\right)^2} s^{1/2}dw,
\\&=
\frac{L^2 \gamma ^2 \sigma^2}{2} s^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty
\underbrace{
\frac{1}{i^{2\alpha}} \int_0^{s^{-1/2}} \frac{w^2 \left(1 + {O}(s + i^{-\alpha}s^{1/2}w)\right)}{\left(1 + (1-s)i^{-\alpha}C(s^{1/2}w)/s + {O}(i^{-\alpha}w^2)\right)^2} dw
}_{U_i(s)}.
\end{align*}

First, $\displaystyle
\frac{C(s^{1/2}w)}{s}  = \frac{-\frac{A^{(2)}}{3}(s^{1/2}w)^3+\frac{A^{(1)}}{2}(s^{1/2}w)^2}{s} \xrightarrow{s \to 0} \frac{A^{(1)}}{2}w^2.
$ For every $i \geq 1$, by the dominated convergence theorem,
\begin{align*}
U_i(s) &= \frac{1}{i^{2\alpha}}\int_0^\infty \frac{w^2 \left(1 + {O}(s + i^{-\alpha}s^{1/2}w)\right)}{\left(1 + (1-s)i^{-\alpha}C(s^{1/2}w)/s + {O}(i^{-\alpha}w^2)\right)^2} \mathbf 1_{[0, s^{-1/2}]}(w)dw,
\\&
\xrightarrow{s\to0} \frac{1}{i^{2\alpha}}\int_0^\infty\frac{w^2}{(1+\frac{A^{(1)}}{2}w^2i^{-\alpha})^2}dw.
\end{align*}

Therefore, using the DCT once again,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^\infty U_i(s) \xrightarrow{s\to0} \sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{1}{i^{2\alpha}} \int_0^\infty\frac{w^2}{(1+\frac{A^{(1)}}{2}w^2i^{-\alpha})^2}dw.
\]

Let $u = \sqrt{\frac{A^{(1)}}{2}i^{-\alpha}}w$.

The integral becomes:
\[
\int_0^{\infty} \frac{\frac{2}{i^{-\alpha}A^{(1)}}\, w^2}{(1+w^2)^2} \sqrt{\frac{2}{i^{-\alpha}A^{(1)}}}\,\mathrm{d}w
=  (i^{-\alpha}\gamma  L)^{-3/2} \int_0^{\infty} \frac{w^2}{(1+w^2)^2}\,\mathrm{d}w = (i^{-\alpha}\gamma  L)^{-3/2} \frac{\pi}{4}.
\]


Therefore
\begin{align*}
\mathcal V(1-s)  - R(1-s) &\sim \frac{L^2 \gamma ^2 \sigma^2}{2} s^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty (L\gamma )^{-3/2} i^{-\alpha/2} \sim \frac{1}{2}(L\gamma )^{1/2} \sigma^2 s^{-1/2} \zeta(\alpha/2)\frac{\pi}{4}.
\end{align*}


Applying the Tauberian theorem with $\omega = 1/2$ yields the $T^{-1/2}$ rate (the $O(1/T)$ term is negligible):
\begin{align*}
V_T &\sim \frac{1}{\Gamma(1/2)} \left[ \frac{\pi}{8} L^{1/2} \gamma ^{1/2} \sigma^2 \zeta\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right) \right] T^{-1/2} = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{8} L^{1/2} \gamma ^{1/2} \sigma^2 \zeta\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right) T^{-1/2}.
\end{align*}

\paragraph{Item 1.}
Write $\widetilde V_T(\gamma )= z(\gamma )\,T^{-r}$, where $z$ is continuous and strictly
positive on the admissible interval and $r\geq0$ does not depend on $\gamma $.
We always have $r<\omega$ (indeed $\omega-r = \omega>0$ for constant, 
$\omega-r=\frac{\beta}{\alpha}>0$ for WSD $\alpha<2$, and
$\omega-r=\frac12+\frac{\beta-1}{\alpha}>0$ for WSD $\alpha>2$).

Fix $\epsilon>0$. On the interval
$[\epsilon,\gamma_{\max})$, the function $z$ attains a minimum $z_\epsilon>0$ since $z(\gamma)\xrightarrow{\gamma\to\gamma_{\max}}\infty$ for constant and $\lim_{\gamma\to\gamma_{\max}}z(\gamma) >0$ for WSD, so
\[
    \forall \gamma  \in [\epsilon, \gamma_{\max}),\quad  \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\gamma )\ \geq \widetilde V_T(\gamma )
    \ \ge\ z_\epsilon T^{-r}.
\]
Choose $x_T=T^{-w}$ with
$w\in\big(0,\,1-\tfrac{r}{\omega}\big)$ (a nonempty interval since $r<\omega$). Then
$x_T\to0$, hence $x_T\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\to0$, and since $z(\gamma )\xrightarrow{\gamma \to0}0$, $z(x_T) =o(1)$.
The simplified equivalents apply:
\[
    \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(x_T)
    = O\big(x_T^{-\omega}T^{-\omega}\big)+z(x_T)T^{-r}
    = O\big(T^{-\omega(1-w)}\big)+o\big(T^{-r}\big)
    = o\big(T^{-r}\big),
\]
both exponents being $>r$ by the choice of $w$.

As a result, for $T$ large enough,
$\displaystyle \min_{\gamma }\widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\gamma )\le \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(x_T)
< \tfrac{z_\epsilon}{2}T^{-r}\le \inf_{\gamma \ge\epsilon}\widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\gamma )$,
so every minimizer lies in $(0,\epsilon)$. Since $\epsilon>0$ is arbitrary, a minimizer of the asymptotic risk satisfies
$\gamma\to0$ as $T \to \infty$.


\paragraph{Item 2.}
We have $\gamma\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\to0$, so the correction
factors in the equivalents of \cref{th:constant,th:wsd} satisfy, near any minimizer $\gamma$ of $\widetilde{\mathcal R}$, which tends to $0$ by item 1,
$1-\gamma \frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)}{3}=1+o(1)$ and $2-c-\gamma \mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)(1-\tfrac{2c}{3})=2-c+o(1)$.

The leading-order risk is obtained by freezing these factors at their $\gamma \to0$ limits:
\[
    \widetilde{\mathcal R}^{(0)}_T(\gamma )=C_B\,\gamma ^{-\omega}\,T^{-\omega}+C_V\,\gamma ^{v}\,T^{-r},
    \qquad C_B,C_V>0,
\]
where the exponents are
\[
\begin{cases}
   v=1 \text{ and } r=0 & \text{for constant schedule},\\
    v=\frac{1}{\alpha} \text{ and } r=1 - \frac{1}{\alpha} & \text{for WSD schedule with } 1 < \alpha <2,\\
     v=r=\frac{1}{2}  & \text{for WSD schedule with } \alpha>2.
\end{cases}
\]

Let us now minimize $\gamma \mapsto \widetilde{\mathcal R}^{(0)}_T(\gamma)$.
It is a smooth function with a unique interior critical point, which gives
\[
    \frac{d}{d\gamma }\widetilde{\mathcal R}^{(0)}_T(\gamma )=0
    \iff \gamma ^{v+\omega}=\frac{\omega\,C_B}{v\,C_V}\,T^{r-\omega}
    \iff \widetilde{\gamma}^*_T=\Big(\frac{\omega\,C_B}{v\,C_V}\Big)^{\frac1{v+\omega}}T^{\frac{r-\omega}{v+\omega}}.
\]

So $\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T = \Theta(T^{-\vartheta})$ where $\vartheta = -\frac{r-\omega}{v+\omega} = \frac{\omega-r}{v+\omega}$.

\paragraph{Item 3.}
Comparing
\cref{th:constant,th:wsd} with $\widetilde{\mathcal R}^{(0)}_T$ term by term,
\[
  \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\gamma) = \varphi_B(\gamma)\,C_B\,\gamma^{-\omega}T^{-\omega}
                    + \varphi_V(\gamma)\,C_V\,\gamma^{v}T^{-r},
\]
where $\varphi_B,\varphi_V$ collect the correction factors
($1-\gamma \frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)}{3}, \kappa(c,\gamma)/(2-c)$, $\kappa_1$, $\kappa_2$, $\mathcal I_{\alpha,\gamma})$, are independent of $T$ and tend to $1$ as $\gamma \to 0$. Therefore, by positivity of all terms for sufficiently large $T$,
\[
  \min\{\varphi_B(\gamma),\varphi_V(\gamma)\}  \widetilde{\mathcal R}^{(0)}_T(\gamma)
  \leq \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\gamma)
  \leq \max\{\varphi_B(\gamma),\varphi_V(\gamma)\}  \widetilde{\mathcal R}^{(0)}_T(\gamma).
\]

Moreover $\lim_{\gamma\to 0}\min\{\varphi_B(\gamma),\varphi_V(\gamma)\}=1$ and $\lim_{\gamma \to0}\max\{\varphi_B(\gamma),\varphi_V(\gamma)\}=1$.
Write $\rho_T:=\inf_\gamma\widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\gamma)$ and
$\rho^{(0)}_T:=\inf_\gamma\widetilde{\mathcal R}^{(0)}_T(\gamma)=\widetilde{\mathcal R}^{(0)}_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T)$.
Let $\gamma_T$ be a minimizer of $\widetilde{\mathcal R}_T$. Then $\gamma_T\to0$ by 1., while by
2., $\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T\to0$. Hence as $T \to \infty$,
\begin{align}
\label{eq:min_eqrisk}
  &\rho_T \leq \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T)
      \leq \max\{\varphi_B(\widetilde{\gamma}^*
      _T),\varphi_V(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T)\} \cdot\widetilde{\mathcal R}^{(0)}_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T)
      = \rho^{(0)}_T\,(1+o(1)),
      \\
  &\rho^{(0)}_T  \leq \widetilde{\mathcal R}^{(0)}_T(\gamma_T)
      \leq \frac{\widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\gamma_T)}{\min\{\varphi_B(\gamma_T),\varphi_V(\gamma_T)\}}  
      = \rho_T\,(1+o(1)).
\end{align}
Therefore $\rho_T\sim \rho^{(0)}_T$, and combining with \cref{eq:min_eqrisk},
$\widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T)\sim \rho^{(0)}_T\sim \rho_T$, which is \cref{lemma:eta_star_to_0}, part 3.

Splitting
\[
   r_{T,i}=(S_{T,i}-1)\,e^{X_{T,i}}+\big(e^{X_{T,i}}-1\big)
\]
and applying the hypotheses,
\[
   |r_{T,i}|
   \le\Big(C_0\,\gamma_T\,i^{-\alpha}+C_1\,\gamma_T\,\tau_T\, i^{-\alpha}\Big)\,
      e^{C_1\gamma_T\tau_T i^{-\alpha}} .
\]
Since $\gamma_T \xrightarrow{T\to\infty}0$, we may further restrict to $T$ large
enough that $C_1\gamma_T\leq\tfrac12$; then $C_1\gamma_T\tau_T i^{-\alpha}\le\tfrac12\tau_T i^{-\alpha}$
for every $i\ge1$, and with $i^{-\alpha}\le1$ and $C:=C_0+C_1$ we obtain, uniformly in
$i\ge1$,
\begin{equation*}
   |r_{T,i}|\le C\,\gamma_T\,(1+\tau_T i^{-\alpha})\,e^{\frac12\tau_T i^{-\alpha}}.
\end{equation*}

body_md:

name: Equivalence of Risks

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $B_T,V_T,\widetilde B_T,\widetilde V_T>0$, the ratio
$\mathcal R_T/\widetilde{\mathcal R}_T$ lies between $B_T/\widetilde B_T$ and
$V_T/\widetilde V_T$. It therefore suffices to bound each of these two ratios.
Let $\tau:=\gamma_T L(2-c)T$. 
\[
   \gamma_T\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{}0
   \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   \tau=(2-c)L\,\gamma_T\,T\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{}\infty.
\]

From the proof of \cref{th:wsd}, the per-coordinate contraction factor is
$\Pi_{T,i}=S_{i,T}\,e^{TI_i}$, where
\[
   S_{i,T}=1+O(\gamma_T i^{-\alpha}),
   \qquad
   I_i=-\,i^{-\alpha}\gamma_T L\,\kappa(c)+O(\gamma_T^2 i^{-2\alpha}),
   \qquad
   \kappa(c)=2-c-\gamma_T\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\big(1-\tfrac{2c}{3}\big).
\]
Both $A^{(1)}_i=2\gamma_T Li^{-\alpha}$ and $A^{(2)}_i=\gamma_T^2\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)Li^{-\alpha}$ are
$O(\gamma_T i^{-\alpha})$ uniformly in $i\ge1$; since
$\gamma_T\to0$, so that for $T$ large enough these quantities are below the radius of convergence of the
expansions of $\log(1-A^{(1)}_i+A^{(2)}_i)$ and of $\int_0^1\log(1-A^{(1)}_i u+A^{(2)}_i u^2)\,du$, and the
two $O(\cdot)$ above are uniform in $i\ge1$. Fix $C_0,C_1>0$ such that, for such $T$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform_OO}
   |S_{i,T}-1|\le C_0\,\gamma_T\, i^{-\alpha},
   \qquad
   |X_i|\le C_1\,\gamma_T\,\tau\, i^{-\alpha},
   \qquad X_i:=TI_i+\tau i^{-\alpha},
\end{equation}
The second bound follows from
$X_i=-i^{-\alpha}\gamma_T LT\,\big(\kappa(c)-(2-c)\big)+O(\gamma_T^2Ti^{-2\alpha})$ together with
$\kappa(c)-(2-c)=-\gamma_T\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)(1-\tfrac{2c}{3})=O(\gamma_T)$ and
$\gamma_T^2Ti^{-2\alpha}=O(\gamma_T\tau i^{-\alpha})$.

We compare $\Pi_{T,i}$ to $e^{-\tau i^{-\alpha}}$, i.e.\ we replace $\kappa(c)$ by its
$\gamma_T\to0$ limit $2-c$, and define $r_{T,i}$ by
\[
   \Pi_{T,i}=(1+r_{T,i})\,e^{-\tau i^{-\alpha}},
   \qquad\text{so that}\qquad
   1+r_{T,i}=S_{i,T}\,e^{X_i}.
\]
Thus \cref{lemma:error_r} gives:
\begin{equation*}
   |r_{T,i}|\le C\,\gamma_T\,(1+\tau i^{-\alpha})\,e^{\frac12\tau i^{-\alpha}}.
\end{equation*}
The three ingredients of $r_{T,i}$ are thus: the normalisation $S_{i,T}-1$, the
Euler--Maclaurin remainder hidden in $I_i$, and the freezing
$\kappa(c)\rightarrow 2-c$. 

 
\paragraph{Bias.}
$B_T(\gamma_T)=\frac{L\Delta}{2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty i^{-(\alpha+\beta)}\Pi_{T,i} = \frac{L\Delta}{2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty i^{-(\alpha+\beta)}(1+r_{T,i})e^{-\tau i^{-\alpha}}$.
Using \cref{eq:uniform_r} of \cref{lemma:error_r}, 
\[
B_T(\gamma_T) = \frac{L\Delta}{2} \left(S_1(\tau) +S_2(\tau)\right)\quad\text{where } S_1(\tau):=\sum_{i=1}^\infty i^{-(\alpha+\beta)}e^{-\tau i^{-\alpha}} \text{ and } S_2(\tau):=\sum_{i=1}^\infty r_{T,i} i^{-(\alpha+\beta)}e^{-\tau i^{-\alpha}}.
\] 

Applying Euler--Maclaurin to $x\mapsto x^{-(\alpha+\beta)}e^{-\tau x^{-\alpha}}$
(with the substitution $u=\tau x^{-\alpha}$, $\mathrm dx=\tfrac1\alpha\tau^{1/\alpha}u^{-1/\alpha-1}\mathrm du$),
\[
   S_1(\tau)=\int_0^\infty x^{-(\alpha+\beta)}e^{-\tau x^{-\alpha}} dx\,(1+o(1))
   =\frac{\tau^{-\omega}}{\alpha}\int_0^\infty u^{\omega-1}e^{-u}
   du\,(1+o(1))
   =\frac{\Gamma(\omega)}{\alpha}\,\tau^{-\omega}\,\bigl(1+\delta(\tau)\bigr),
\]
with $\omega=\tfrac{\beta-1}{\alpha}+1$ and $\delta(\tau)\xrightarrow{\tau\to\infty}0$
the (sum $\to$ integral) discrepancy. This is exactly the $\gamma$-free
content of the Tauberian step of \cref{th:wsd}, read here as a plain Laplace
asymptotic. In particular $\frac{\alpha\,\tau^{\omega}}{\Gamma(\omega)}S_1(\tau)=1+\delta(\tau)$. Note that extending the lower bound of the continuous integral from $1$ to $0$ introduces a residual error $\int_0^1 x^{-(\alpha+\beta)}e^{-\tau x^{-\alpha}}\,\mathrm dx$. Because of the exponential term, this residual decays exponentially as $O(e^{-\tau})$ and is therefore safely absorbed into the $1+o(1)$ asymptotic equivalence. 

The correction to $S_1(\tau)$ is $S_2(\tau)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}i^{-(\alpha+\beta)}e^{-\tau i^{-\alpha}}r_{T,i}$.
Using \cref{eq:uniform_r}, the factor $\gamma_T$ pulls out and it remains to compare
\[
   \sum_{i=1}^\infty  i^{-(\alpha+\beta)}(1+\tau i^{-\alpha})\,e^{-\frac12\tau i^{-\alpha}} \quad \text{to } S_1(\tau).
\]
Applying Euler--MacLaurin again, the whole sum is still $O(\tau^{-\omega})$.
Therefore
\[
   \frac{\alpha\,\tau^{\omega}}{\Gamma(\omega)}S_2(\tau) = \frac{\alpha\,\tau^{\omega}}{\Gamma(\omega)}\sum_{i=1}^\infty \frac{e^{-\tau i^{-\alpha}}}{i^{\alpha+\beta}}\,r_{T,i}=O(\gamma_T).
\]
Combining $S_1(\tau)$ and $S_2(\tau)$,
$\frac{\alpha\tau^\omega}{\Gamma(\omega)}\sum_i i^{-(\alpha+\beta)}\Pi_{T,i}=1+\delta(\tau)+O(\gamma_T)$,
so $B_T(\gamma_T)=\frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha}\Gamma(\omega)\tau^{-\omega}(1+\delta(\tau)+O(\gamma_T))$.
On the other hand \cref{th:wsd} gives
$\widetilde B_T(\gamma_T)=\frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha}\Gamma(\omega)\,[\gamma_T L\kappa(c)T]^{-\omega}
=\frac{L\Delta}{2\alpha}\Gamma(\omega)\,\tau^{-\omega}\,(1+O(\gamma_T))$,
the last equality because $[\kappa(c)/(2-c)]^{-\omega}=1+O(\gamma_T)$. Dividing,
\[
   \frac{B_T(\gamma_T)}{\widetilde B_T(\gamma_T)}=1+O(\gamma_T)+\delta(\tau).
\]

\paragraph{Variance.}
$V_T = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^{T-1}
   \frac{L^2}{i^{2\alpha}}\gamma_T^2\eta_k^2\sigma^2
   \prod_{m=k+1}^{T-1}\!\left[1-2\bar\nu_m\frac{L}{i^\alpha}\right] = V^A_T+V^B_T,$
where 
\begin{itemize}
      

        \item Regarding the constant part $V_T^A$,
        \begin{align*}
        V_T^A
        &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^{(1-c)T}
           \frac{L^2\gamma_T ^2\sigma^2}{i^{2\alpha}}
           [1-A^{(1)}_i+A^{(2)}_i]^{(1-c)T-k}
           \exp\!\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{cT-1}
           \log\!\left(1-A^{(1)}_i\frac{\ell}{cT}+A^{(2)}_i\!\left(\frac{\ell}{cT}\right)^{\!2}\right)\right],
        \\&= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty \sum_{k=0}^{(1-c)T}
           \frac{L^2\gamma_T ^2\sigma^2}{i^{2\alpha}}
           (A^{(3)}_i)^{(1-c)T-k}(1+r^A_{T,i})\,e^{-\kappa_2 Ti^{-\alpha}}, \quad (\text{$A^{(3)}_i$ consists in two geometric sums)}
           \\&= 
           \frac{L\gamma_T ^2\sigma^2}{4\bar\gamma_T}\sum_{i=1}^\infty  i^{-\alpha}
           (1+r^A_{T,i}) \left[e^{-\kappa_2 Ti^{-\alpha}} - e^{-\kappa_1 Ti^{-\alpha}} \right] = S_1 + S_2,
        \end{align*}
        where $r^A_{T,i}$ satisfies $|r^A_{T,i}| \leq C\gamma_T (1+\kappa_2 T i^{-\alpha})e^{\frac12 \kappa_2 T i^{-\alpha}} $ (\cref{lemma:error_r}) with $\tau$ replaced by $\kappa_2 T \leq \tau$; and $S_2$ the term containing $r_{T,i}^A$.

        By Euler-Maclaurin,
        $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} i^{-\alpha} e^{-\kappa T i^{-\alpha}} = \frac{\Gamma\left(1 - \frac{1}{\alpha}\right)}{\alpha} (\kappa T)^{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}} (1 + \delta'(T))$.
        We have $S_1= \widetilde V_T^A (1+\delta'(T))$ and $S_2 = O(\gamma_T)S_1$, so $\frac{V_T^A}{\widetilde V_T^A} = 1+O(\gamma_T) +\delta'(T)$.
            

        \item For $\alpha<2$, regarding the cooldown part $V_T^B$, denoting $x=\frac{\ell}{cT}$,
        \begin{align*}
        V_T^B
        &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty \sum_{\ell=1}^{cT-1}
        \frac{L^2\sigma^2}{i^{2\alpha}}
           \!\left(\gamma_T \frac{\ell}{cT}\right)^{\!2}
           \exp\!\left[\sum_{j=1}^{\ell-1}
           \log\!\left(1-A^{(1)}_i\frac{j}{cT}+A^{(2)}_i\!\left(\frac{j}{cT}\right)^{\!2}\right)\right],
        \\&=
        \frac{L^2\sigma^2\gamma_T^2}{2}\sum_{i=1}^\infty i^{-2\alpha}\sum_{\ell=1}^{cT-1}
        x^2
        (1+r^B_{T,i,\ell})\exp\bigg[{-cTi^{-\alpha}\underbrace{\gamma_TLx^2\left(1-\frac{\gamma_T\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)x}{3}\right)}_{=:\psi_T(x)}}\bigg],
        \end{align*}
        where $r^B_{T,i,\ell}$ obeys the bound of \cref{lemma:error_r} with $\tau$ replaced by $cT\psi_T(x)$. The bound stays uniform as $cT\psi_T(x) \leq \kappa_2T\leq \tau$. \cref{as:eta} gives $\gamma_T\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda) <2$ so $\frac13\gamma_TLx^2 \leq \psi_T(x)\leq \gamma_TLx^2$ for $x \in [0,1]$. Moreover,
        \[
        \sum_{\ell=1}^{cT-1}
        x^2e^{-cTi^{-\alpha}\psi_T(x)}=cT\int_0^1 x^2 e^{-cTi^{-\alpha}\psi_T(x)}dx \cdot (1+O(1/T))).
        \]
        The Riemann sum over $i$ is made possible with a step size of $(\gamma_T L cT)^{-1/\alpha}$ that tends to 0 since $\gamma_TT \to \infty.$ The integral converges if $\alpha<2$, assumed here.
        By the same decomposition $(S_1,S_2)$ with $S_2 = O(\gamma_T)S_1$, we get $\frac{V^B_T}{\widetilde V^B_T}=1+O(\gamma_T) + \delta_\alpha''(T)$.

        \item For $\alpha>2$, reading the proof of \cref{th:wsd} ($c=1$) with $\gamma_T$ explicit and
        keeping the finite upper limit $s^{-1/2}$, the substitution $u=s^{1/2}w$ gives the
        per-mode contribution
        \[
           v^B_i(T)=\tfrac{\sqrt\pi}{8}\sigma^2 L^{1/2}\gamma_T^{1/2}T^{-1/2}\,i^{-\alpha/2}\,F(\theta_i)\,(1+O(\gamma_T)+O(1/T)),
           \qquad \theta_i:=\gamma_T L\,i^{-\alpha}T,
        \]
        where $F(\theta):=\tfrac{4}{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^{\sqrt\theta}y^2e^{-y^2}\mathrm dy$ increases from
        $F(0)=0$ to $\lim_{\theta \to \infty}F(\theta)=1$, and the $o(1)$ (Euler--Maclaurin) is uniform. Since
        $\widetilde V^B_T=\tfrac{\sqrt\pi}{8}\sigma^2 L^{1/2}\gamma_T^{1/2}\zeta(\tfrac\alpha2)T^{-1/2}$
        replaces every $F(\theta_i)$ by $1$,
        \[
           \frac{V^B_T}{\widetilde V^B_T}
           =1-\underbrace{\frac{1}{\zeta(\alpha/2)}\sum_{i\ge1}i^{-\alpha/2}\bigl(1-F(\theta_i)\bigr)+O(\gamma_T)+O(1/T)}_{=:-\delta''(\gamma_T,T)}.
        \]
        \[
           |\delta''(\gamma_T,T)|
           =\frac{1}{\zeta(\alpha/2)}\sum_{i\ge1}i^{-\alpha/2}\bigl(1-F(\theta_i)\bigr) +o(1).
        \]
        Since $\gamma_TT\to\infty$, for each fixed $i$,
        $1-F(\theta_i)\to0$. Dominated by the summable $i^{-\alpha/2}$ ($\alpha/2>1$),
        DCT gives $|\delta''(\gamma_T,T)|\to0$. Denote $|\delta''(\gamma_T,T)|$ by $\delta_\alpha''(T).$
    \end{itemize}


Hence $V_T/\widetilde V_T=1+O(\gamma_T)+\delta'(T)+\delta_\alpha''(T)$ with $\delta'(T)$ and $\delta_\alpha''(T)$ that tend to 0 as $T\to \infty$.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
Collecting both ratios,
\[
   \epsilon_T(\gamma_T)=
   O(\gamma_T) + o(1).
\]
Hence, $\epsilon_T(\gamma_T)\to 0$.

\textbf{Constant schedule.} The bias is treated as above with $\tau := 2\bar\gamma_T L T$, since $\Pi_{T,i} = (1 - 2\bar\gamma_T L i^{-\alpha})^T$. For the variance, $V_T/V_\infty = 1 - \zeta(\alpha)^{-1}\sum_{i} i^{-\alpha}(1-2\bar\gamma_T L i^{-\alpha})^T = 1 - O\big((\gamma_T T)^{1/\alpha - 1}\big) \to 1$ since $\gamma_T T \to \infty$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We recall the definitions:
\[\left\{\begin{aligned}
\bar\nu_k &:= \frac{2\gamma_T\eta_k - \gamma_T^2\eta_k^2\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)}{2} = \gamma_T\eta_k - \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\gamma_T^2\eta_k^2, \\
\Pi_{T,i} &:= \prod_{k=0}^{T-1} \left[ 1 - 2\bar\nu_k \frac{L}{i^\alpha} \right].
\end{aligned}\right.\]

Knowing that $\forall x \in[0,1/2], \; -2x \leq \log(1-x)\leq -x$, we can bound $\Pi_{T,i}=\exp(\sum_k\log(1-2\bar\nu_k L i^{-\alpha}))$ for $i$ sufficiently large so that $\forall k, \,2\bar\nu_k L i^{-\alpha } \leq 1/2$. We denote $i_{\min}$ the index from which it is satisfied. It is independent of $T$ and $\gamma_T$ since $\forall k, 2L\bar\nu_k \leq \frac{L}{\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)} = \frac{1}{\zeta(\alpha)}\leq1$.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bounds_Pi}
\exp\left( \sum_{k=0}^{T-1} -4Li^{-\alpha}\bar\nu_k \right) \leq \Pi_{T,i} \leq \exp\left( \sum_{k=0}^{T-1} -2Li^{-\alpha}\bar\nu_k  \right) .
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Constant schedule.}

\begin{itemize}
\item By \cref{eq:bounds_Pi} We have 
\[B_T \geq  \frac12\sum_{i\geq i_{\min}} L\Delta i^{-\alpha-\beta} \exp(-4Li^{-\alpha} T\bar\gamma_T),
\]with $\bar\gamma_T = \bar\nu_0$. Therefore, to obtain $B_T\to 0$, we must have $T\bar\gamma_T \to \infty$. Since the term $- \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)\gamma_T^2\eta_k^2$ is negative, this requires $T\gamma_T \to \infty$.
\item For the variance, if we keep only the last term of the sum over $k$, with $\prod_k (1-2\bar\nu_k)$ equal to 1,
\[
\displaystyle V_T \geq \frac12 \sum_{i\geq i_{\min}}  L^2 i^{-2\alpha} \gamma_T^2 \sigma^2. 
\]
Therefore we must have $\gamma_T \to 0$.

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{WSD schedule.}

First, let $\ell = T-k$.

If $\displaystyle \ell \geq cT, \quad \sum_{j=1}^{\ell-1}\eta_{j+k} = \underbrace{\frac{cT}{2}}_{\text{decay part}} + \underbrace{(\ell - cT)}_{\text{constant part}}$. If $\ell < cT$ there is only a decay part so $cT/2$ is an upper bound. Moreover, $\frac{\ell^2}{2cT}-(\ell- \frac{cT}{2})= \frac{cT}{2}(\frac{\ell}{cT}-1)^2 \geq 0$. Therefore:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:slope}
\sum_{j=k+1}^{T-1}\eta_j = \sum_{j=1}^{\ell-1}\eta_{j+k} \leq \frac{\ell^2}{2cT}.
\end{equation}

\begin{itemize}
\item  Let us show that $\gamma_T T \to \infty$.

We have $\bar\nu_k \leq \gamma_T \eta_k$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\eta_k \leq T$. Since $\exp$ is increasing, \cref{eq:bounds_Pi} gives
\[B_T \geq  \frac12\sum_{i\geq i_{\min}} L\Delta i^{-\alpha-\beta} \exp\left(-4Li^{-\alpha} \sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\bar\nu_k\right) \geq \frac12\sum_{i\geq i_{\min}} L\Delta i^{-\alpha-\beta} \exp\left(-4Li^{-\alpha} T \gamma_T\right),
\]
So, to have $B_T\to 0$, we find the same conclusion $T\gamma_T \to \infty.$

\item Let us show that $\gamma_T \to 0$. Suppose first $\alpha<2$.
Using \cref{eq:slope},
\begin{align*}
\displaystyle V_T &\geq \frac12 \sum_{i\geq i_{\min}}  L^2 i^{-2\alpha} \gamma_T^2 \sigma^2\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\eta_k^2 \prod_{j=k+1}^{T-1}[1-2\bar\nu_j],
\\
&\stackrel{\labelcref{eq:bounds_Pi}}{\geq}
\frac12 \sum_{i\geq i_{\min}}  L^2 i^{-2\alpha} \gamma_T^2 \sigma^2\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\eta_k^2 \exp\left( \sum_{j=k+1}^{T-1} -4Li^{-\alpha}\bar\nu_j\right),
\\
&\stackrel{\labelcref{eq:slope}}{\geq} \frac12 \sum_{i\geq i_{\min}}  L^2 i^{-2\alpha} \gamma_T^2 \sigma^2\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\eta_k^2 \exp\left( -2Li^{-\alpha}\gamma_T\frac{(T-k)^2}{cT} \right).
\end{align*}

We index the sum on the decay part from $\ell=\lceil cT/2 \rceil$ to $\ell=\lfloor cT \rfloor$, and on dimensions $i\geq i_{\min}$ greater than $\gamma LcT$. Let $i_{\min}'(\gamma LcT) := \max\{i_{\min}, (2\gamma L c T)^{1/\alpha}\}$. 

For $i \geq i_{\min}'(\gamma LcT),\; 2Li^{-\alpha} \gamma \frac{\ell^2}{cT} \leq \left(\frac{\ell}{cT}\right)^2$ and $\frac{\ell}{cT}\leq 1$ , so 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exponent}
\displaystyle \exp\left( -2Li^{-\alpha}\gamma\frac{\ell^2}{cT} \right) \geq \exp \left(- \bigg(\frac{\ell}{cT}\bigg)^2\right) \geq 1/e.
\end{equation}
Therefore, as all terms are positive:
\begin{align*}
V_T 
&\geq \frac12 \sum_{i\geq i_{\min}}  L^2 i^{-2\alpha} \gamma_T^2 \sigma^2\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}\eta_{T-\ell}^2 \exp\left( -2Li^{-\alpha}\gamma_T\frac{\ell^2}{cT} \right),
\\
&\stackrel{\labelcref{eq:exponent}}{\geq} \frac12 \sum_{i\geq i'_{\min}(\gamma_T LcT)}  L^2 i^{-2\alpha} \gamma_T^2 \sigma^2\sum_{\ell=\lceil cT/2 \rceil}^{\lfloor cT \rfloor}\frac{\eta_{T-\ell}^2 }{e} \quad\text{and}\displaystyle \quad \eta_{T-\ell}=\frac{\ell}{cT}\geq\frac12 \text{ on the block}, \\
&\geq \frac{\sigma^2\gamma_T^2L^2}{2e}\left(\sum_{\ell=\lceil cT/2\rceil}^{\lfloor cT\rfloor}\frac14\right)\sum_{i\geq i'_{\min}(\gamma_T LcT)}i^{-2\alpha},
\\
&\geq \frac{\sigma^2\gamma_T^2L^2\,cT}{32\,e}\int_{i'_{\min}(\gamma_T LcT)}^{\infty}x^{-2\alpha}dx
\ =\ \frac{\sigma^2\gamma_T^2L^2\,cT}{32\,e\,(2\alpha-1)}\,(i'_{\min}(\gamma_T LcT))^{1-2\alpha} ,
\\&
\geq \frac{\sigma^2\gamma_T^2L^2\,cT}{32\,e\,(2\alpha-1)}\,(2\gamma_T LcT)^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} \quad \text{ for }\gamma_T T \text{ large enough so that } i_{\min}'(\gamma_TLcT)=(2\gamma_TLcT)^{1/\alpha},\\
&= \frac{2^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}}\sigma^2L^{1/\alpha}}{32\,e\,(2\alpha-1)}\gamma_T^{1/\alpha} (cT)^{\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}}.
\end{align*}

\item Suppose $\alpha>2$. 

We now keep only the dimension $i=i_{\min}$, and index the sum on the decay part over the
block $\ell \in \left[\tfrac12 A^{-1/2},\, A^{-1/2}\right]$, where
$A := \frac{2Li_{\min}^{-\alpha}\gamma_T}{cT}$ is such that the exponent equals $A\ell^2$.
This block is contained in $\{1,\dots,\lfloor cT\rfloor\}$ and contains at least
$\tfrac14 A^{-1/2}$ integers, since $\gamma_T T \to \infty$ gives $A^{-1/2}\leq cT$ and
$\gamma_T L \leq \frac{2}{\zeta(\alpha)} \leq 2$ gives $A^{-1/2}\geq 4$ for $T$ large enough.


For $\ell$ in this block,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exponent_big_alpha}
\exp\left( -2Li_{\min}^{-\alpha}\gamma_T\frac{\ell^2}{cT} \right) = \exp\left(-A\ell^2\right) \geq 1/e
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\eta_{T-\ell}^2 = \left(\frac{\ell}{cT}\right)^2 \geq \frac{1}{4A(cT)^2}.
\end{equation}
Therefore, as all terms are positive,
\begin{align*}
V_T
&\stackrel{\labelcref{eq:exponent_big_alpha}}{\geq}
\frac{L^2 i_{\min}^{-2\alpha}\gamma_T^2\sigma^2}{2}\frac{1}{e}\frac{A^{-1/2}}{4}\frac{1}{4A(cT)^2}
\ =\ \frac{L^2 i_{\min}^{-2\alpha}\sigma^2}{32\,e}\,\frac{\gamma_T^2\,A^{-3/2}}{(cT)^2},
\\
&=\ \frac{i_{\min}^{-\alpha/2}L^{1/2}\sigma^2}{2^{13/2}\,e}\ \gamma_T^{1/2}\,(cT)^{-1/2},
\end{align*}
using $A^{-3/2}=\left(2Li_{\min}^{-\alpha}\right)^{-3/2}\gamma_T^{-3/2}(cT)^{3/2}$, together with
$2-\tfrac32=\tfrac12$ and $-2+\tfrac32=-\tfrac12$.


\item \emph{Conclusion for $\alpha <2$ and $\alpha>2$.}
Remind that by \cref{cor:epsilon}, $\mathcal R_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T) \sim \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T)$.

This gives $\mathcal R_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T) = O(T^{-q})$ with 
$q=\begin{cases}
\frac{\alpha+\beta-1}{\alpha+\beta} & \text{if }\alpha<2,
\\
\frac{2\alpha+2\beta-2}{3\alpha+2\beta-2} & \text{if } \alpha>2.
\end{cases}$

Combining with the bounds above yields $\gamma_T = O(T^{-\alpha q + \alpha - 1})$ if $\alpha <2$ and $\gamma_T = O(T^{1-2q })$ if $\alpha >2$, which gives $\gamma_T = O(T^{-\vartheta})$ where $\vartheta$ is the exponent defined \cref{lemma:eta_star_to_0} verifying $\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T = \Theta(T^{-\vartheta})$. In particular, $\gamma_T \to 0$ and $\gamma_TT\to \infty$.

\end{itemize}

Let us combine the preceding lemmas. Let $(\gamma_T)$ a sequence which satisfies 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ccl_risks}
\mathcal R_T(\gamma_T)\leq\mathcal R_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T)(1 + o(1)).
\end{equation}
\begin{itemize}
\item
\cref{eq:ccl_risks} implies $\mathcal R_T(\gamma_T) = O(\mathcal R_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T))$. By \cref{lemma:bounds}, $\gamma_T\to 0$ and $\gamma_T T \to \infty$.
\item
By \cref{lemma:uniform_epsilon}, we have therefore $\mathcal R_T(\gamma_T) \sim \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\gamma_T)$. 
\item
By \cref{cor:epsilon}, $\mathcal R_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T) \sim \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T)$.
\item
By \cref{lemma:eta_star_to_0}, item 3., $\widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T)\sim \min_\gamma \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\gamma)\leq \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\gamma_T)$, so $\widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\gamma_T) \geq \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T)(1+o(1)).$
\end{itemize}

So $\mathcal R_T(\gamma_T) \sim \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\gamma_T) \geq \widetilde{\mathcal R}_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T)(1+o(1)) \sim \mathcal R_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T)(1+o(1)) .$ 

Knowing \cref{eq:ccl_risks}, we get $\mathcal R_T(\gamma_T) \sim \mathcal R_T(\widetilde{\gamma}^*_T)$.

Taking the derivative of this expression with respect to $c$ yields:
\[
    h'(c) = \frac{1}{4\alpha}\Gamma\left(1-\frac{1}{\alpha}\right) (2-c)^{-2} \underbrace{\left[ \frac{2-2\alpha+\alpha c}{2-\alpha} c^{\frac{1-2\alpha}{\alpha}} (2-c)^{\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}} - 1 \right]}_{=: w(c)-1}.
\]
For $c \in (0,1)$,
\begin{itemize}
\item If $c \leq \frac{2\alpha-2}{\alpha}$:\quad $\frac{2-2\alpha+\alpha c}{2-\alpha}\leq 0$ so $w(c)-1 <0$.
\item If $c > \frac{2\alpha-2}{\alpha}$:\quad $w(c)>0$ and
\[
\frac{w'(c)}{w(c)} = \frac{\alpha^2 c(2-c) + (2-2\alpha+\alpha c)(2-4\alpha+\alpha c)} {\alpha c(2-c)(2-2\alpha+\alpha c)} >0.
\]
Therefore $w$ increases so $w(c) < \lim_{c\to1}w(c) =1$. Thus, $h'(c) < 0$.
\end{itemize}

Consequently, $c<1 \Rightarrow h'(c) < 0$ while $h'(1)=0$, which implies that $h$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $(0, 1].$
